why_how.text: You must yield to emergency vehicles from any direction, and where you stop matters as much as stopping.
A police stop has its own steps, and mixing them up with the emergency vehicle rule is a common slip.

scenario.text: You are crossing an intersection when you hear a siren behind you.

reasoning.text: You may never stop inside an intersection, so you clear it, then move as close to the right side as is safe.

result.text: You stop at the right side, stay stopped until the vehicle passes, then keep at least five hundred feet behind it.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you can follow right behind an emergency vehicle once it passes.

correction.text: You must keep at least five hundred feet behind an emergency vehicle after it has gone by.

memory_support.text: Siren: right, stop, wait, then stay back.

prompt.text: After an ambulance with its siren on passes you, how far back must you stay?

answer.text: At least five hundred feet behind it.

rationale.text: The manual says that once an emergency vehicle has gone by, you keep at least five hundred feet behind it.

lines.text: Police stops have their own steps.

narration.text: This lesson covers two situations every driver meets sooner or later: an emergency vehicle coming through with its light or siren on, and a police officer signaling you to stop. You must yield to emergency vehicles such as fire trucks, police vehicles and ambulances when they approach from any direction with a light or siren on. Police stops follow a separate set of steps. We will take each in turn, then compare them, because the two procedures overlap in some places and differ in others, and that difference is what learners most often confuse.

When you see or hear an emergency vehicle warning, move right away as close to the right side of the road as is safe, and stop. The one place you must never stop is inside an intersection, so if you are in one, you clear it first. Do not drive or stop in any way that gets in the emergency vehicle's path. Then stay stopped until it has passed or until an officer tells you to move. Those are the full steps: right side, stop, keep out of its path, and wait for it to pass or for an officer's direction. Pulling right and stopping is the core of the rule.

lines.text: Keep at least five hundred feet back.

narration.text: Once the emergency vehicle has gone by, you can pull back into traffic, but you may not tuck in right behind it. The manual sets a minimum gap: you must keep at least five hundred feet behind an emergency vehicle after it passes. That distance applies to every emergency vehicle that has just gone by with its light or siren, whether it is a fire truck, a police vehicle or an ambulance. If several drivers pull out at once, each of them owes the same five hundred feet, so leave the space and let the emergency vehicle pull well ahead before you settle into your own speed.

lines.text: Not in an intersection or median.

narration.text: A police vehicle trying to stop you will turn on flashing lights or a siren. When that happens, pull as far to the right as is safe, stop, and turn off the engine. Two places are off limits: do not stop in an intersection, and do not pull onto a highway's center median. Once you are stopped, keep your own movements and your passengers' movements to a minimum. Keep your hands on the steering wheel, and have your passengers keep their hands in plain view. These steps let the officer approach a car whose occupants are calm and easy to see.

lines.text: Police stop adds engine off and hands.

narration.text: Here is where drivers mix things up. For an emergency vehicle, you pull right and stay stopped until it passes or an officer waves you on. For a police stop, you also turn off the engine and keep your hands on the wheel. The places to avoid differ too. Pulling over for an emergency vehicle, you avoid stopping in an intersection. Pulling over for police, you avoid an intersection and also a highway center median. Keep the two lists separate: the police stop adds the engine, the hands and the center median to the emergency vehicle steps.

Here is a quick check: an ambulance with its siren on has just passed you, and you are ready to pull back into your lane. How far behind it must you stay? The answer is at least five hundred feet. That gap is required once any emergency vehicle has gone by. It is easy to remember the pull-over steps and forget this last one, because the danger seems to be over once the vehicle passes. The manual still sets the distance, so you leave at least five hundred feet between you and the emergency vehicle after it passes. That is the rule.

lines.text: Do not argue at the stop.

narration.text: A few last steps complete a police stop. Show your driving privilege or registration only when the officer asks, and stay inside the vehicle unless you are asked to get out. If the stop happens after dark, turn on your interior light once you have stopped and before the officer reaches you. And do not argue with the officer at the stop, because traffic violations and traffic crimes charged against you are decided in court. Together with yielding to emergency vehicles and staying five hundred feet back, that gives you the full picture for lights and sirens.

why_how.text: Work zones put workers and equipment close to traffic, which is why fines are doubled and the speed applies at all times.
Flaggers and automated flagger devices give signals you must read correctly, especially on two-lane roads.

scenario.text: You enter a work zone on a Sunday morning and see no workers or equipment, only orange signs and a temporary speed sign.

reasoning.text: A temporary work zone speed applies at all times, even when no workers can be seen.

result.text: You keep to the temporary limit until an End Work Zone Speed Limit sign or a different posted speed limit.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a work zone speed only counts when workers are visible.

correction.text: The temporary speed applies at all times, so an empty work zone is no reason to speed back up before the end sign.

memory_support.text: Orange means slow, all the time, fines doubled.

prompt.text: On a two-lane work zone road, an automated device shows a flashing yellow light with its arm up. Should you stop or go?

rationale.text: You stop while the red light is on and the arm is down, and you go when the yellow flashes and the arm is up.

lines.text: Workers may be close to traffic.

narration.text: Work zones are marked by orange traffic control devices, and inside them workers and construction equipment may be working close to traffic. That closeness is why the rules here are strict. Traffic fines are doubled in every work zone, and drivers are expected to yield to workers. In this lesson we will look at how you are guided through a zone, how the temporary speed works and when it ends, how flaggers and automated flagger devices direct you on two-lane roads, and what changes when the work zone is on a freeway instead.

Several tools guide you through a work zone: signs, cones, flaggers and lane markings. Each has a job. Orange signs warn you of what is ahead, so you know early that the road changes. Orange cones steer you away from the construction itself. Flaggers and lane markings tell you where to go when the normal lanes are not available. Read each one as part of a single path through the zone. If you follow the signs for what is coming and the cones for where to drive, you stay clear of the work and of the people doing it. Follow them in order.

lines.text: Even with no workers in sight.

narration.text: A temporary speed posted in a work zone applies at all times, even when no workers can be seen. Day or night, weekday or weekend, the posted temporary limit is the limit. It also has a clear end point. The lower work zone limit holds until a sign ends it, either an End Work Zone Speed Limit sign or a different posted speed limit. So you do not decide on your own that the zone is over because the cones thin out or the equipment is parked. You keep the lower speed until you pass the sign that ends it. Weekends and nights included.

lines.text: No workers is not a reason to speed.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver enters a work zone on a quiet evening, sees no workers and no machines, and speeds back up to the normal limit. That is wrong. A work zone with no workers in sight still carries its temporary speed limit, so an empty work zone is no reason to speed back up before the end sign. Remember too that fines in every work zone are doubled. The only things that end the lower limit are an End Work Zone Speed Limit sign or a different posted speed limit, not the absence of people. Keep the lower speed until the sign that ends it.

lines.text: Flaggers or automated devices may stop you.

narration.text: On two-lane roads, expect to be stopped in work zones by flaggers or by automated devices. Flaggers use signs and hand signals to tell you which way to go, to slow down or to stop. An automated flagger device does the same job as a human flagger and has red and yellow lights plus a stop arm. At an automated flagger, stop while the red light is on and the arm is lowered, and go when the yellow light flashes and the arm is raised. It does not use a green light signal, so a flashing yellow with the arm raised is your signal to go.

lines.text: Fewer or narrower lanes; expect to merge.

narration.text: Freeway work zones work differently. Flaggers and automated devices are what you meet on two-lane road work zones, while on freeways you usually keep driving through. The lanes may be fewer, narrower or newly placed, and you should expect to merge. Freeway work zones can also put you very close to cones, workers and equipment, so slow down and pay attention. Construction vehicles may be driving in the zone too. Do not follow construction vehicles while you are in a work zone, and expect them to enter the road and slow traffic.

Here is a quick check: you reach an automated flagger device on a two-lane road. Its yellow light is flashing and its arm is raised. What do you do? The answer is to go. You stop while the red light is on and the arm is down, and you go when the yellow light flashes and the arm is up. Do not sit waiting for a green light, because the device has red and yellow lights and a stop arm, and it does not use a green light signal. Flashing yellow with the arm raised is the go signal. Red with the arm down is the only stop signal.

lines.text: Stop on red, go on flashing yellow.

narration.text: Let us pull the work zone rules together. Orange traffic control devices mark the zone, and workers may be close to traffic, so fines are doubled and you yield to workers. Orange signs warn of what is ahead and orange cones steer you away from the work. The temporary speed applies at all times, workers or not, until an end sign or a different posted limit. On two-lane roads, flaggers and automated devices may stop you; on freeways you usually keep moving through fewer or narrower lanes. And never follow construction vehicles inside the zone.

why_how.text: Railroad signs, signals and markings each tell you something different, and only some of them require you to stop.
Trains are closer than they look and cannot stop quickly, so the never-do rules at tracks protect your life.

scenario.text: You see a railroad advance sign, then a crossbuck assembly with a stop sign beneath it at the tracks.

reasoning.text: The advance sign only warns that a crossing is ahead, while the crossbuck carries a stop sign you must obey.

result.text: You slow at the advance sign and come to a stop at the crossbuck.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a railroad advance sign means you must stop right there.

correction.text: The advance sign only warns that a crossing is ahead; the crossbuck at the crossing carries the yield or stop sign.

memory_support.text: Look, listen, slow; never stop, never race.

prompt.text: Which part of a railroad crossing carries the yield or stop sign you must obey?

rationale.text: A crossbuck assembly includes a yield or stop sign you must obey, while the advance sign only warns of the crossing.

narration.text: Railroad crossings are marked with signs and signals, and the moment you see them the manual gives you three actions: look, listen and slow down, because you may need to stop. This lesson walks through each warning in the order you meet it on the road, from the first sign well before the tracks to the signals and pavement markings at the crossing itself. Then we will cover the rules about never stopping on the tracks or racing a train, and why the size and speed of a train are so easy to misjudge. Every crossing deserves that attention.

The first warning is the railroad advance sign. It warns that a railroad crossing is ahead. At the crossing itself you meet the railroad crossbuck assembly. It includes a yield or stop sign that you must obey, and where there are several tracks, a sign under the crossbuck shows how many. So the advance sign is your early notice, and the crossbuck is where the actual rule applies. The number of tracks matters too, because more tracks means more places a train can come from and more distance to clear before you are safely across.

Many crossings also have a crossing signal system. It has flashing red lights and may have a gate with flashing red lights that activate when a train is near. On the pavement before the crossing you will see markings of a large X with the letters RR. Together with the signs, these give you several separate warnings. Each one is telling you the same thing in a different way: a railroad crossing is close, a train could be coming, and you need to slow down, look and listen so you are ready to stop. Treat each one as a reason to be ready.

Here is the trap: treating the advance sign and the crossbuck as the same thing. A railroad advance sign only warns that a crossing is ahead, while the crossbuck assembly at the crossing carries a yield or stop sign that you must obey. A driver who stops at the advance sign is stopping too early, and a driver who rolls through a crossbuck stop sign because it looks like just another warning is breaking the rule. Slow down at the warning, and obey the yield or stop sign that is part of the crossbuck at the tracks. Keep the two signs separate.

lines.text: Cross only if you can clear.
Never try to beat a train.

narration.text: Three rules keep your vehicle out of a train's path. First, cross the tracks only when you are sure your vehicle can clear the crossing completely; if traffic is backed up past the tracks, stay where you are until there is room. Second, never stop on the tracks. Third, never try to race a train to a crossing. The reason is simple: a train you see is closer than it appears, and trains cannot stop quickly. And at a crossing, one train can hide a second train from your view, so a passing train does not mean the tracks are clear.

lines.text: School buses and hazmat vehicles stop.

narration.text: Some vehicles stop at every railroad crossing whether or not a train is coming. School buses, hazmat vehicles and some school activity vehicles must stop at every railroad crossing. That matters when you are behind one. If you are following a school bus or a hazmat truck toward the tracks, be ready to stop when it does, and leave yourself room to do so smoothly. A sudden stop ahead of you at a crossing is not a surprise; it is the rule for those vehicles, so you plan for it. Following at a distance gives you time to stop smoothly behind it.

Here is a quick check: on the way to a railroad crossing you pass a railroad advance sign, and at the tracks there is a crossbuck assembly. Which one carries the yield or stop sign that you must obey? The answer is the crossbuck assembly. The advance sign only warns that a crossing is ahead, while the crossbuck includes a yield or stop sign you must obey, plus a sign showing the number of tracks when there are several. Slow down at the warning, and follow the yield or stop sign at the crossbuck. Obey the crossbuck every time.

lines.text: Never stop on or race the tracks.

narration.text: To wrap up the railroad warnings, remember the order you meet them in. When you see railroad crossing signs or signals, look, listen and slow down, because you may need to stop. The railroad advance sign warns that a crossing is ahead. At the crossing, the crossbuck assembly carries a yield or stop sign that you must obey, with a sign under it showing how many tracks there are. Never stop on the tracks and never try to race a train, because a train you see is closer than it appears, trains cannot stop quickly, and one train can hide a second train from your view.

title.text: Stopping at crossings and getting stuck

why_how.text: You must know exactly where to stop and which conditions require a stop at a railroad crossing.
If your vehicle is ever stuck on the tracks, the order of your actions decides whether you get away safely.

scenario.text: Your car stalls on the tracks and no train is in sight.

reasoning.text: You first get out of the vehicle, then move away from the tracks even if no train is in sight.

result.text: Once away, if it is safe, you use the ENS sign on a post near the tracks to tell the railroad about the blockage.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you should call the railroad from inside a stuck car before getting out.

correction.text: Getting out and away comes before notifying the railroad at the ENS sign, and notifying is done only if it is safe.

memory_support.text: Get out, get away, then the ENS sign.

prompt.text: At a crossing with no stop line, how far from the nearest rail must you stop?

rationale.text: When you must stop at a crossing, you stop at the stop line, or if there is none, at least fifteen feet from the nearest rail.

narration.text: This lesson is about the moment at a railroad crossing when you have to stop, and the rare moment when something goes wrong on the tracks. First we will set where to stop. Then we will list the conditions that require a stop, including one that applies even when no train is in sight. After that comes the rule about crossing gates and how to start across safely. Finally we will walk through the exact order of steps when a vehicle, a person or an object is stuck on the tracks, which is the part people most often get backwards.

lines.text: Stop line, or fifteen feet from the rail.
Flashing lights or a near train.

narration.text: When you must stop at a railroad crossing, stop at the stop line, or if there is none, at least fifteen feet from the nearest rail. You must stop before the tracks when the flashing red lights are on, or when a train is clearly visible or so near that crossing would be hazardous. You must also stop when a stop sign is posted, even with no train in sight, and when a flagger signals you to stop. A posted stop sign means you stop every time, while flashing red lights, a visible close train or a flagger signal are the other triggers.

title.text: The gate and the second train

lines.text: Never go around or under a gate.
Look both ways at multiple tracks.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A train passes, the gate begins to rise, and a driver decides it is safe to slip around the gate. Driving around or under a crossing gate while it is down, rising or lowering is illegal and extremely dangerous. After stopping at a crossing, start across only when you are sure it is safe. Where there are multiple tracks, look both ways for a second train on another track before you go. A gate that is still moving and a second set of tracks are both reasons to keep waiting. Being sure it is safe is the only signal to start across.

lines.text: Move away, even with no train.
Use the ENS sign if safe.

narration.text: If a vehicle, person or object is stuck on the tracks, first get out of the vehicle, then move away from the tracks even if no train is in sight. Only after that, and only if it is safe, find the Emergency Notification System, or ENS, sign on a post near the tracks and use it to tell the railroad about the blockage so it can warn trains. If a train is coming while you are stuck, move away at a forty-five degree angle from the tracks toward the direction the train is coming from, so flying debris does not hit you. Those steps always come in that order.

Here is a quick check: you are required to stop at a railroad crossing, but there is no stop line painted on the road. How far from the nearest rail must you stop? The answer is at least fifteen feet. Where there is a stop line, you stop at the stop line; where there is none, you stop at least fifteen feet from the nearest rail. Either way you stay well clear of the tracks, and you start across only when you are sure it is safe, looking both ways at multiple tracks for a second train. The stop line, when there is one, always comes first.

To finish, keep the order straight. If you are stuck on the tracks, getting out and away comes before notifying the railroad at the ENS sign, and notifying is done only if it is safe. If a train is approaching, move away at a forty-five degree angle toward the direction it is coming from. At every crossing, stop at the stop line or at least fifteen feet from the rail when required, stop for flashing lights, a near train, a posted stop sign or a flagger, and never go around or under a gate. That order is the heart of this lesson.

why_how.text: Streetcars and light rail trains share city streets with cars and stop often for passengers, so they need room and patience.
Turning, parking and changing lanes near tracks each come with specific rules.

scenario.text: A streetcar ahead of you stops to let passengers on and off.

reasoning.text: When a streetcar or train stops for passengers, you stay behind it until it moves again or the people are safely clear.

result.text: You wait behind the streetcar instead of passing it.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a stopped streetcar can be passed like a stopped car.

correction.text: A stopped streetcar loading passengers is a reason to stay behind it, not to pass, until it moves or the riders are safely away.

memory_support.text: Streetcars go first; never turn across one.

prompt.text: A streetcar going your way is stopped in the lane beside you. May you turn across its path?

rationale.text: You never turn across the path of a streetcar or train moving your way in the next lane, even while it is stopped.

narration.text: Some cities run streetcars and light rail trains right on their streets. They are electric transit vehicles on tracks set in the street. They sometimes share lanes with cars, and they stop often for passengers, much like buses. Because they run on fixed tracks, they cannot steer around you, and because of their size they cannot stop quickly. This lesson covers who goes first, what to do when one stops for passengers, how to park and open doors near the tracks, and the turning and lane change rules that keep you out of their way.

lines.text: Stay behind one that is loading.

narration.text: Always let streetcars and light rail trains go first, and do not try to pass one unless it is safe. When a streetcar or train stops to let people on or off, stay behind it until it moves again or the people are safely clear. Watch for riders near streetcar and train stops, since passengers may dash across lanes to catch one, and follow pedestrian signals so people can cross safely. Approaching tracks at an intersection, stay behind any stop line before you cross the tracks. Each of these rules gives the streetcar and its riders room.

lines.text: A stopped streetcar is not a pass.
Wait until it moves or riders clear.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A streetcar stops in front of you, and it looks just like a car stopped in traffic, so a driver swings around it. A stopped streetcar loading passengers is a reason to stay behind it, not to pass, until it moves again or the riders are safely away. People are stepping on and off, and some may be crossing the lanes to reach it. The right move is to wait behind the streetcar. Patience here protects the passengers, and it keeps you from turning or merging in front of a vehicle that cannot stop quickly.

lines.text: Stay behind the solid white line.

narration.text: Tracks are never a parking spot. Leave your car behind the solid white line that marks off the track area, or where there is no line, close to the curb and as far from the rails as possible. Make sure your parked vehicle is fully clear of the tracks. And before you open a door, check for approaching streetcars or trains. A door swung open into the track area can be struck, so the check comes first. Parking a little farther from the rails always beats leaving any part of your vehicle where a streetcar has to pass. Clear of the tracks is the goal.

lines.text: Never turn across one in the next lane.
Wait for a left turn signal.

narration.text: Turning is where streetcar crashes happen. Never turn across the path of a streetcar or train moving your way in the next lane, even while it is stopped. Do not turn in front of an approaching streetcar or light rail train unless it is safe, and slow down and look both ways before crossing tracks at an intersection. When turning across tracks, look both ways for streetcars and signal your turn, and where a left turn signal is present, wait for the left turn signal before turning left over the tracks. Turning across tracks always calls for a careful look.

lines.text: It is stopped. Can you turn?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a streetcar moving your way is stopped in the lane beside you, and you want to turn across its path. May you make the turn? The answer is no. You never turn across the path of a streetcar or train moving your way in the next lane, even while it is stopped. A stopped streetcar can start moving again, and it cannot stop quickly once it does. So you wait for it to go, look both ways before crossing the tracks, and wait for the left turn signal where there is one. Waiting for it to move on is the safe choice every time.

Two last rules round out this lesson. Check for streetcars and trains before changing lanes, since one may be close behind you, and avoid sudden braking or surprise moves around them because they cannot stop quickly. If your vehicle ever touches a streetcar or train, wait for the operator or the police to tell you what to do. With those added to letting streetcars go first, staying behind one that is loading, parking clear of the tracks and never turning across one in the next lane, you have every rule from this lesson.
